description: We're a team from a student science club at the Medical University of Gdańsk, with backgrounds in medicine and biotechnology and a shared interest in space medicine. We bring the clinical side; we're looking for teammates with skills in Python, data science/ML, UI/UX, or wearable signal processing (ECG, HRV). Curious about space and physiology? Join us!
summary: Crew Health Monitoring System is a web app prototype that helps astronauts on a Mars mission look after their own health when messages to Earth take up to 22 minutes. Each crew member logs in with their avatar and sees a clickable body map (head, chest, abdomen, arms, legs) color-coded as normal, watch or alert, with the main problems and next steps shown beside it. Around it are modules based on the NASA Human Research Program hazards: a daily wellbeing check-in with ways to improve mood and a breathing exercise, a countermeasure exercise plan and radiation tracking that detects solar storms automatically from onboard proton readings, triggers a shelter alert and adds the dose to each astronaut’s career total. It also contains information about medication reminders and cfDNA as a novel tissue-specific damage biomarker which could be used with nanopore sequencing. Every mission day is logged automatically, and one click produces a report for the flight surgeon on Earth. Because the communication delay rules out real-time medical support, crews need tools that catch problems early and tell them what to do. The demo uses simulated crew data based on published NASA research. It is a concept prototype.
details:
What it does
Crew Health Monitoring System is a web app for astronauts on an 860-day Mars mission. It runs on a live mission clock: each day is added to the log automatically, and the app always shows the current mission day, phase (transit, Mars surface, return), signal delay to Earth and ship time. Each crew member logs in by tapping their avatar.

The home screen shows a body map (head and neck, chest, abdomen, arms, legs). Each region is marked normal, watch or alert with a color, an icon and a label. Around the map are tiles for the other modules and a “To do today” list.

  • Body regions: measurements linked to known spaceflight risks, each with a status, a trend and recommended actions. Examples are optic disc swelling (SANS), jugular vein flow (thrombosis risk), sleep, reaction time, VO₂max, heart rate variability, urinary calcium (kidney stones), hip bone density, calf muscle volume, skin and hand injuries after spacewalks, and balance after landing.
  • Blood and cfDNA: a liquid biopsy panel. Cell-free DNA methylation patterns show which tissue the DNA comes from, so each tissue’s signal is shown as a change from the crew member’s own pre-flight sample, with thresholds at 1.5× and 3×. Samples are taken weekly, plus an extra one after each solar storm.
  • Mind: a daily check-in of eight questions that takes under a minute. It gives a wellbeing score with a 14-day trend and suggests ways to improve mood that the astronaut can add to a personal plan. It includes a guided box-breathing exercise and advises other activities to help with mental health.
  • Medication: reminders that take meals into account (on an empty stomach, with food, after food, before sleep). Each dose can be marked as taken, overdue doses are flagged, and as-needed medications are logged.
  • Exercise: a daily countermeasure plan with built-in timers. It changes with the mission phase: cycle ergometer, resistance device and treadmill with a harness in flight, weighted training on Mars, supervised balance work after landing.
  • Radiation: shows onboard proton readings (>10 MeV) from the last 72 hours. When the flux passes 10 pfu (NOAA S1), the app records a solar storm by itself, classifies it from S1 to S4, raises a shelter alert and adds the dose to each astronaut’s career total, compared with NASA’s 600 mSv limit.
  • Report: one click creates a text summary for the flight surgeon on Earth.

Benefits and intended impact
With up to 22 minutes of one-way delay, a Mars crew can’t rely on real-time help from Earth. The app supports Earth-independent medical care. It gathers scattered data into one view, catches problems early and tells the crew what to do next. It also saves crew time and bandwidth, because the flight surgeon receives one concise report. The same approach could help in remote places on Earth, such as polar stations, ships and rural clinics.

How we built it
Our team is three medical and biotechnology students with no programming experience. We defined the medical content, features and requirements. The code was written with Claude at our direction. The app is a single file of HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, with SVG graphics and no external libraries. Data is saved in the browser. We tested it on desktop screen sizes.

What makes it creative
It combines cfDNA tissue-of-origin analysis with everyday self-care in one tool. It detects solar storms automatically from ship sensor readings. Its advice takes the signal delay into account, and the interactive body map makes the data easy to understand at a glance.

Factors we considered
Signal delay, limited crew time, status shown with more than color alone, mobile use, and keeping blood draws to a minimum. All crew data in the demo is simulated. The project builds on NASA Human Research Program hazards and risks. It is only a concept prototype.
